Welcome to my building.

This city represents a community. Each building may look simple from the outside, but there are many different stories inside. The building in the centre represents me. Scroll down to explore the experiences and memories that shaped who I am.

“How do we learn to live together?” — Daniel Heath Justice

Childhood Memories

When I was younger, my whole family lived together, but as I got older, there was a time when I lived mostly with my father. Because he often worked late, I spent a lot of time by myself. From the outside, that might have seemed like freedom, but it also meant that my daily habits became unhealthy. I stayed up too late, played games for too long, and did not always take care of myself properly.

One memory that stayed with me was when my father came home late from work and caught me playing video games all night. He was very upset, and at the time, I mostly felt scared and embarrassed. Later, I understood why that moment mattered. It was not only about playing games. It helped me realize that the way I live affects not only me, but also the people who care about me. That experience taught me that responsibility is connected to family, and that improving myself can also help the people around me feel happier and less worried.

I did not know yet that the world outside this room would one day ask a lot of me.

My father lit the candles. For a moment, we were all in the same place at the same time.

I wore what my culture gave me. I did not yet know how far I would carry it.

I had a place I belonged to. I had people who cheered for me.

These were the people I left behind. They do not know that I still think about them.

The last time I stood on a stage in Korea. I did not know it was a goodbye.

Why We Moved

People may know that I moved from Korea to Canada, but they may not know why my family made that decision. There were several reasons, but one of the main reasons was that my older brother had a very difficult experience in the Korean school system and struggled to feel accepted there. My family believed that moving to Canada could give him a chance to start again in a different environment.

Even though the decision was mainly focused on my brother, it completely changed my life as well. I had to leave my friends, adjust to a new country, and learn how to express myself in English. Looking back, I realize that a decision made because of one family member can shape the lives of everyone in the family.

The last trip we took together before leaving. At the time, it felt normal, but now I see it as one of the last memories from my life in Korea.

I looked down at a city I did not know yet. Somewhere below was the life I was about to start.

Language

Sometimes people may think I am quiet, but speaking in English has not always been easy for me. There have been many times when I knew what I wanted to say but needed more time to express it clearly.

Learning to communicate in a different language has made me more patient with myself. It has also reminded me that people may have thoughts, feelings, and ideas that they cannot easily show from the outside. Someone who seems quiet may still have a lot to say.

My elementary graduation. A chapter closed. I did not know what the next one would look like.

My friends made this for me on graduation day. For the first time, I felt like I had a name here.

A trip to Ottawa with my mom. Just the two of us. Some moments do not need a reason.

Friends and Community

Moving to Canada changed the way I thought about community. I lost daily contact with many of my friends in Korea and had to build new friendships in Canada.

This experience taught me that belonging can change over time. Some relationships may become less active when people are far apart, but that does not mean they stop mattering. I also learned that my new communities have become important without replacing the old ones. Because of this, I now understand that a person can feel connected to more than one place and more than one group of people.

Golf tryout with Kyle. I showed him how to juggle golf balls. I was starting to feel less alone.

Mr. Guest, who was my favourite coach and teacher, passed away that week. I wore black every day. It was the only thing I knew how to do.

The day of my storytelling presentation. I have never been more nervous in my life.

Final Reflection

My artifact points to the question “How do we learn to live together?” because it shows that people cannot be fully understood from the outside alone. In my city, the buildings may look simple from far away, but each one holds different stories inside. The building in the centre represents me, and moving through it shows the different layers of my life. This connects to the course idea that storytelling helps people become visible to each other. Many parts of my life, like moving from Korea to Canada, learning English, and building new communities, are not things people can see right away. My artifact gives people a way to look closer and understand more than what they first notice. This idea also connects to Medicine Walk. Franklin only begins to understand Eldon after listening to the stories Eldon has carried for many years. In the same way, my artifact shows that learning to live together starts with listening, looking beyond first impressions, and remembering that every person has a deeper story inside them.
